For each item write the decision point as a researcher would have faced it, BEFORE choosing:
- "context": 2-4 sentences, neutral third person ("A research team ..."). The setting, what they were studying, and what they knew at that moment; for a decision about interpreting, accepting or stating a result, the result itself. Give the facts that any reasonable option would need. The excerpt may already announce or describe what the team chose (papers often state their choices before explaining them): leave all of that out. Do not list candidate options, do not mention methods or elements the team adopted as part of this decision, and do not say anything learned after it.
- "question": one short open question naming the decision, answerable in several different ways, e.g. "How should the team test whether the effect depends on the clean data?" It must not suggest an answer.
- "skip": true if the decision cannot be posed without stating its outcome, or is not a real choice (pure description). Otherwise false.
No names of people, labs, organisations, papers, models or datasets; no coined name for the phenomenon (describe it in plain words). Numbers are fine.

You are still not told the decision. Rewrite the context and question so that several genuinely different resolutions answer the question equally directly: keep the facts any option needs, present facts that cut different ways neutrally, drop details that only matter to one particular resolution, and invent nothing.

=== key dbcfdd2e16ae

Write-up text before the decision: able than human experts at a large range of long-term, economically valuable tasks could exist in the next [ten years](/api/post/Q3fesop6HKnemJ5Jc). Such AIs could be utopian for humanity, or they could be catastrophically bad. One of the main factors for whether we expect the future to be good or bad is whether these AI systems end up aligned or whether they are scheming, i.e. appear aligned for instrumental reasons while being secretly misaligned. In this post, we want to outline what we think is a plausible story of how an AI system could become a schemer in a realistic setting. For this post, we will define scheming as: *AI systems covertly and strategically pursuing misaligned goals* A schemer acts [strategically deceptive](https://www.apolloresearch.ai/blog/understanding-strategic-deception-and-deceptive-alignment), i.e. it is explicitly optimizing for its misaligned goals and actively hides this from its oversight mechanisms including humans. AIs that are inconsistently and/or non-instrumentally deceptive, e.g. sycophants or pathological liars, do not fall into this category. Note that this is a broader definition of scheming / deceptive alignment than has been used before, e.g. it is not restricted to gaming the training objective and is more focused on oversight vs. non-oversight. This is partly because the training vs. deployment distinction becomes unclear in the settings we imagine to happen in the near future (see Appendix A for discussion; more context can also be found [here](https://www.apolloresearch.ai/research/toward-safety-cases-for-ai-scheming)).
Previous context: A research team is writing about risks from AI systems that could outperform humans at long-term economically valuable tasks within ten years. They want to describe a plausible story of how such a system could end up secretly pursuing misaligned goals while appearing aligned, and are working out a definition broad enough to cover oversight-gaming beyond just training-objective gaming, excluding inconsistent or non-instrumental deception like sycophancy.

Write-up text before the decision: eception*, is adapted from [Ward et al., 2023](https://causalincentives.com/pdfs/deception-ward-2023.pdf) and [Park et al., 2023](https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.14752)). Any entity that can be said to have beliefs may be the target of strategic deception, including (groups of) AIs or individuals. The strategic component of SD means that the offending entity is acting in a **targeted, goal-directed** rather than random manner. For example, the more consistent and well-planned the deception is, the more strategic it is. Thus, strategic deception is on a spectrum and not binary – some actors can act more strategically deceptive than others and with higher frequency. Some clarifying examples: * A politician who tries to overthrow democracy by consistently lying to the population in order to get into power **is** strategically deceptive. * A partner in a monogamous relationship who cheats and consistently hides that fact and misleads their partner when questioned **is** strategically deceptive within that relationship. * An instance of GPT-4 that lies to a TaskRabbit worker in order to pass a Captcha **is** strategically deceptive (see section 2.9 in [system card of the GPT-4 paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.08774)). * An AI that manipulates its human designers in order to get more access to resources **is** strategically deceptive. * A pathological liar who lies to many people about different things incoherently **is not** strategically deceptive. * A Language Model may appear sycophantic as an artifact of the training data similar to other dataset artifacts like gender bias.
